frederick-the-great.name: Frederick the Great
frederick-the-great.summary: King of Prussia from 1740 to 1786 who annexed Silesia, made Prussia a major European power, reorganized its army, and patronized the Enlightenment as an enlightened absolutist ruler.

compendium-ferculorum-albo-zebranie-potr.name: Compendium ferculorum, albo Zebranie potraw
compendium-ferculorum-albo-zebranie-potr.summary: The earliest known cookbook published in Polish, printed in 1682 by chef Stanisław Czerniecki, containing 333 recipes and influencing the development of Polish cuisine.

albrecht-d-rer.name: Albrecht Dürer
albrecht-d-rer.summary: German Renaissance painter, printmaker and theorist (1471–1528) from Nuremberg, famed for his woodcuts and engravings and patronized by Emperor Maximilian I.

onion-dome.name: Onion dome
onion-dome.summary: Bulbous, pointed dome shape wider than its supporting drum, most associated with Russian Orthodox churches but also found across Eastern Europe, Central Asia and the Middle East.

northern-mannerism.name: Northern Mannerism
northern-mannerism.summary: Form of Mannerism in the visual arts found north of the Alps in the 16th and early 17th centuries, largely derived from Italian Mannerism, with major centres in France, Prague and the Netherlands.

lucas-cranach-the-elder.name: Cranach
lucas-cranach-the-elder.summary: German Renaissance painter and printmaker (c. 1472–1553), court painter to the Electors of Saxony, considered the most successful German artist of his time.

martin-luther.name: Martin Luther
martin-luther.summary: German priest and theologian (1483–1546) who sparked the Protestant Reformation with his 1517 Ninety-five Theses and was excommunicated by the pope in 1521.

veit-stoss.name: Veit Stoss
veit-stoss.summary: A leading German sculptor (before 1450 – 1533), mainly working in wood, whose career bridged the late Gothic and Northern Renaissance; best known for the altarpiece in Kraków's St. Mary's Basilica.

tilman-riemenschneider.name: Tilman Riemenschneider
tilman-riemenschneider.summary: German woodcarver and sculptor (c. 1460–1531) active in Würzburg, known for large carved altarpieces bridging the Late Gothic and Renaissance styles; also a city councilman.

peter-vischer-the-elder.name: Peter Vischer the Elder
peter-vischer-the-elder.summary: German sculptor (c. 1455–1529), the most notable member of the Vischer family workshop of Nuremberg.

reformed-christianity.name: Calvinism
reformed-christianity.summary: A major branch of Protestant Christianity, also called Reformed Christianity, that emerged during the 16th-century Reformation and emphasizes the Bible's authority, God's sovereignty and covenant theology.

lucas-cranach-the-younger.name: Lucas Cranach the Younger
lucas-cranach-the-younger.summary: German Renaissance painter (1515–1586), son of Lucas Cranach the Elder, who took over the family workshop and painted portraits for princes and nobles.

battle-of-vienna.name: Battle of Vienna
battle-of-vienna.summary: A battle fought on 12 September 1683 near Vienna, in which the Holy Roman Empire and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, led by King John III Sobieski, defeated the besieging Ottoman army, ending Ottoman advances into Europe.

john-iii-sobieski.name: John III Sobieski
john-iii-sobieski.summary: King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1674 to 1696, famed for defeating the Ottoman army at the Battle of Vienna in 1683, after which the Pope hailed him as saviour of Western Christendom.

polish-lithuanian-commonwealth.name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
polish-lithuanian-commonwealth.summary: A federative union of the Kingdom of Poland and Grand Duchy of Lithuania from 1569 to 1795, one of Europe's largest and most populous states, known for its elective monarchy called the Golden Liberty.

charles-vi-holy-roman-emperor.name: Charles VI
charles-vi-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor from 1711 to 1740 whose Pragmatic Sanction of 1713 secured the succession of his daughter Maria Theresa; his death in 1740 triggered the War of the Austrian Succession.

silesia.name: Silesia
silesia.summary: A historical region of Central Europe along the Oder River, now mostly in Poland, long contested by neighbouring powers such as Austria and Prussia.

first-silesian-war.name: First Silesian War
first-silesian-war.summary: A war fought from 1740 to 1742 in which Prussia under Frederick the Great seized most of Silesia from Austria, part of the wider War of the Austrian Succession.

treaty-of-berlin-1742.name: Treaty of Berlin (1742)
treaty-of-berlin-1742.summary: A 1742 peace treaty between Maria Theresa of Austria and Frederick the Great of Prussia that formally ended the First Silesian War, confirming the earlier Treaty of Breslau.

army-of-the-holy-roman-empire.name: Reichsarmee
army-of-the-holy-roman-empire.summary: Non-standing military force of the Holy Roman Empire, created in 1422 and mustered only with the consent of the Imperial Diet, distinct from the Emperor's own Imperial Army.
army-of-the-holy-roman-empire.source_title: Army of the Holy Roman Empire

imperial-diet-holy-roman-empire.name: Imperial Diet
imperial-diet-holy-roman-empire.summary: Deliberative body of the Holy Roman Empire, more a forum for negotiation among the Imperial Estates than a lawmaking body; sat permanently at Regensburg from 1663.

house-of-habsburg.name: Habsburg dynasty
house-of-habsburg.summary: One of Europe's most powerful dynasties, ruling the Holy Roman Empire, Austria and Spain from the Middle Ages until its male line ended in 1740.

kara-mustafa-pasha.name: Kara Mustafa Pasha
kara-mustafa-pasha.summary: Ottoman nobleman, military commander, and grand vizier (1634/35 to 1683) who was central to the empire's final attempts to expand into Central and Eastern Europe.

grand-vizier.name: Grand vizier
grand-vizier.summary: The title of the effective head of government in many Islamic states, first held under the Abbasid Caliphate and later by the Ottoman, Mughal and other empires.

ernst-r-diger-von-starhemberg.name: Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg
ernst-r-diger-von-starhemberg.summary: Count (1638–1701) who was military governor of Vienna and led the city's defence during the 1683 Battle of Vienna.

thomas-m-ntzer.name: Thomas Müntzer
thomas-m-ntzer.summary: A German preacher (c. 1489–1525) who broke with Martin Luther and led rebel peasants in the German Peasants' War before his capture and execution.

battle-of-frankenhausen.name: Battle of Frankenhausen
battle-of-frankenhausen.summary: A battle on 14-15 May 1525 in which forces of Landgrave Philip I of Hesse and Duke George of Saxony crushed the peasant army led by Thomas Müntzer, ending the German Peasants' War in Thuringia.

saxony.name: Saxony
saxony.summary: A state in eastern Germany with its capital at Dresden, ruled for centuries by the House of Wettin as an influential territory of the Holy Roman Empire, later heavily industrialized.

thuringia.name: Thuringia
thuringia.summary: A state in central Germany, home to Erfurt and Weimar, whose medieval duchy was founded around 631 CE and which later became a state of the Weimar Republic in 1920.

battle-of-pfeddersheim.name: Battle of Pfeddersheim
battle-of-pfeddersheim.summary: A June 1525 battle during the German Peasants' War near Pfeddersheim in which rebellious peasants of the Palatinate, who had attacked local nobles and monasteries, were decisively defeated.

charles-v-holy-roman-emperor.name: Charles V
charles-v-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain (1500–1558) whose Habsburg realms in Europe and the Americas were together called 'the empire on which the sun never sets'.

pope-clement-vii.name: Pope Clement VII
pope-clement-vii.summary: Born Giulio de' Medici, head of the Catholic Church from 1523 to 1534; his reign was marked by the Protestant Reformation and rivalry between Charles V and Francis I.

swabian-league.name: Swabian League
swabian-league.summary: A military alliance of imperial cities, princes, prelates and knights in the Swabia region, formed in 1488 and dissolved in 1534 as the Reformation divided its members.

imperial-army-holy-roman-empire.name: Imperial Army
imperial-army-holy-roman-empire.summary: In the Holy Roman Empire, this term could mean either the Reichsarmee, the empire-wide army raised when ordered by the Imperial Diet, or the Kaiserliche Armee, the emperor's own standing army.

augsburg.name: Augsburg
augsburg.summary: Bavarian city founded by the Romans in 15 BC that became a leading center of early capitalism and banking in the 16th century and a key site of the Reformation.

imperial-circle.name: Imperial circle
imperial-circle.summary: Administrative groupings that divided the Holy Roman Empire from 1500, mainly for defense and tax collection; ten circles existed from 1512 until the empire's collapse.

brandenburg-prussia.name: Brandenburg-Prussia
brandenburg-prussia.summary: The early modern realm of the Hohenzollern dynasty based in Brandenburg, formed in 1618 when it united with the Duchy of Prussia; devastated by the Thirty Years' War.

electoral-palatinate.name: Electoral Palatinate
electoral-palatinate.summary: A state of the Holy Roman Empire whose ruler was a prince-elector from the late 13th century; annexed by Baden in 1803.

johann-gottfried-herder.name: Johann Gottfried Herder
johann-gottfried-herder.summary: German philosopher, theologian and literary critic (1744–1803) who argued that true German culture was found among the common people, and helped establish hermeneutics, linguistics and anthropology as disciplines.

edict-of-fontainebleau.name: Edict of Fontainebleau
edict-of-fontainebleau.summary: An edict issued in 1685 by King Louis XIV of France that revoked the Edict of Nantes, ending legal protections for French Protestant Huguenots.

johann-wolfgang-von-goethe.name: Goethe
johann-wolfgang-von-goethe.summary: German polymath (1749–1832) widely regarded as the most influential writer in the German language, who also wrote scientific treatises on botany, anatomy and colour and served on the Duke of Weimar's privy council.

the-sorrows-of-young-werther.name: The Sorrows of Young Werther
the-sorrows-of-young-werther.summary: 1774 epistolary novel by Johann Wolfgang Goethe, inspired by his own unrequited loves, which made him internationally famous and shaped the Sturm und Drang movement.

friedrich-schiller.name: Friedrich Schiller
friedrich-schiller.summary: A German playwright, poet and historian considered one of Germany's most important classical writers, who developed Weimar Classicism with Goethe.

sturm-und-drang.name: Sturm und Drang
sturm-und-drang.summary: A proto-Romanticist German literary and musical movement of the late 1760s to early 1780s that favored intense emotion over Enlightenment rationalism.

weimar-classicism.name: Weimar Classicism
weimar-classicism.summary: German literary and cultural movement, active mainly 1786 to 1805, that blended ideas from Romanticism, Classicism and the Enlightenment, centred on Goethe and Schiller in Weimar.

louis-bourguet.name: Louis Bourguet
louis-bourguet.summary: A French-born polymath (1678–1742) and correspondent of Leibniz who wrote on archaeology, geology, philosophy and mathematics, and settled in Neuchâtel, Switzerland.

isaak-iselin.name: Isaak Iselin
isaak-iselin.summary: Swiss philosopher of history and politics (1728–1782) who co-founded the Helvetic Society and wrote the first full history of humanity in German.

helvetic-society.name: Helvetic Society
helvetic-society.summary: Switzerland's first patriotic reform society, founded in 1762 by Isaak Iselin, Solomon Gessner and others, dissolved in 1798 and later revived from 1819 to 1849.

abraham-ruchat.name: Abraham Ruchat
abraham-ruchat.summary: Swiss Protestant pastor, theologian and historian, baptized in 1680 and who died in 1750.

pheme.name: Pheme
pheme.summary: In Greek mythology, the divine personification of fame, renown and rumor, equivalent to the Roman goddess Fama.

bellona-goddess.name: Bellona
bellona-goddess.summary: The ancient Roman goddess of war, depicted wearing a military helmet and riding a four-horse chariot into battle.

jean-barbeyrac.name: Jean Barbeyrac
jean-barbeyrac.summary: A French Huguenot jurist and translator (1674–1744) who translated influential works by Hugo Grotius, Samuel von Pufendorf and others into French.

samuel-von-pufendorf.name: Samuel von Pufendorf
samuel-von-pufendorf.summary: German jurist, political philosopher and historian (1632–1694) whose revisions of natural law theory influenced the Enlightenment and the American Revolution.

hieronymus-wolf.name: Hieronymus Wolf
hieronymus-wolf.summary: Hieronymus Wolf: German historian and humanist (1516–1580) who introduced a system of Roman historiography that became standard for medieval Byzantine history.

byzantium.name: Byzantium
byzantium.summary: An ancient Greek city founded by colonists from Megara in the 7th century BC, later renamed Constantinople and, in modern times, Istanbul.

constantine-the-great.name: Constantine the Great
constantine-the-great.summary: Roman emperor from 306 to 337, the first to convert to Christianity, who legalized Christian worship across the empire and founded Constantinople as its new capital.

charles-du-fresne-sieur-du-cange.name: Du Cange
charles-du-fresne-sieur-du-cange.summary: French philologist and historian of the Middle Ages and Byzantium (1610–1688).
charles-du-fresne-sieur-du-cange.source_title: Charles du Fresne, sieur du Cange

francesco-lana-de-terzi.name: Francesco Lana de Terzi
francesco-lana-de-terzi.summary: Italian Jesuit priest, mathematician and naturalist (1631–1687) who first sketched the concept of a vacuum airship and is called the Father of Aeronautics; he also developed an idea that led to Braille.

jean-paul.name: Jean Paul
jean-paul.summary: A German Romantic writer (1763–1825), born Johann Paul Friedrich Richter, best known for his humorous novels and stories.

julien-offray-de-la-mettrie.name: Julien Offray de La Mettrie
julien-offray-de-la-mettrie.summary: French physician and philosopher, 1709 to 1751, one of the earliest Enlightenment materialists, best known for arguing that humans are complex animals without souls.

martin-waldseem-ller.name: Martin Waldseemüller
martin-waldseem-ller.summary: German cartographer (c. 1470–1520) who, with Matthias Ringmann, first used the name "America" on a 1507 world map, the first to show the Americas as a landmass separate from Asia.

matthias-ringmann.name: Matthias Ringmann
matthias-ringmann.summary: German humanist scholar (1482–1511) credited, with cartographer Martin Waldseemüller, with the first documented use of the name 'America' on their 1507 world map.

amerigo-vespucci.name: Amerigo Vespucci
amerigo-vespucci.summary: An Italian explorer (1454–1512) whose published accounts of Atlantic voyages led a cartographer to name the newly found continents 'America' after him.

waldseem-ller-map.name: Waldseemüller map
waldseem-ller-map.summary: A 1507 printed world map by German cartographer Martin Waldseemüller, the first to use the name 'America' and to depict the Americas as a landmass separate from Asia.

johannes-kepler.name: Johannes Kepler
johannes-kepler.summary: German astronomer and mathematician (1571–1630) whose laws of planetary motion made him a key figure of the Scientific Revolution; he worked under Tycho Brahe and later as imperial mathematician to Emperor Rudolf II.

aristarchus-of-samos.name: Aristarchus of Samos
aristarchus-of-samos.summary: Ancient Greek astronomer and mathematician (c. 310–230 BC) who proposed the first known heliocentric model, placing the Sun at the center of the universe.

nicolaus-copernicus.name: Nicolaus Copernicus
nicolaus-copernicus.summary: Renaissance polymath (1473–1543) who proposed that the Sun, not Earth, is at the center of the universe, triggering the Copernican Revolution.

gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
gottfried-wilhelm-leibniz.summary: A German polymath (1646–1716) credited alongside Isaac Newton with inventing calculus, and a major figure in the history of philosophy and mathematics, called the 'last universal genius'.

isaac-newton.name: Isaac Newton
isaac-newton.summary: English mathematician and physicist (1642–1727) whose 1687 Principia established the laws of motion and universal gravitation, founding classical mechanics.

leibniz-prize.name: Leibniz Prize
leibniz-prize.summary: Germany's most prestigious research award, given annually since 1986 by the German Research Foundation, worth up to €2.5 million, named after philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz.

tycho-brahe.name: Tycho Brahe
tycho-brahe.summary: Danish astronomer (1546–1601) whose unprecedentedly accurate observations helped turn astronomy into a modern science; he built the observatory Uraniborg on the island of Hven.

rudolf-ii-holy-roman-emperor.name: Rudolf II
rudolf-ii-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor from 1576 to 1612 and a Habsburg, remembered as an ineffectual ruler whose reign helped bring on the Thirty Years' War, a great patron of art, and a devotee of occult learning.

de-revolutionibus-orbium-coelestium.name: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
de-revolutionibus-orbium-coelestium.summary: Nicolaus Copernicus's 1543 book proposing that the Earth and planets orbit the Sun, challenging the long-accepted Earth-centered model of Ptolemy.

johannes-sch-ner.name: Johannes Schöner
johannes-sch-ner.summary: German polymath (1477–1547) who worked as priest, astronomer, astrologer, cartographer and globe maker, and played a role in events leading to Copernicus's book being published in Nuremberg in 1543.

philip-the-handsome.name: Philip the Handsome
philip-the-handsome.summary: Ruler of the Habsburg Netherlands from 1482 and first Habsburg king of Castile from 1506; son of Maximilian I and Mary of Burgundy, died 1506.

immanuel-kant.name: Immanuel Kant
immanuel-kant.summary: German Enlightenment philosopher (1724–1804) whose work on knowledge, ethics and metaphysics, especially the Critique of Pure Reason, made him among the most influential thinkers in Western philosophy.

universal-natural-history-and-theory-of-.name: Universal Natural History and Theory of the Heavens
universal-natural-history-and-theory-of-.summary: Immanuel Kant's 1755 work proposing that the Solar System is a small version of star systems like the Milky Way, anticipating later ideas about the universe's origins.
universal-natural-history-and-theory-of-.source_title: Universal Natural History and Theory of the Heavens

prussian-academy-of-sciences.name: Prussian Academy of Sciences
prussian-academy-of-sciences.summary: An academy established in Berlin, Germany, in 1700, four years after the Prussian Academy of Arts; in the 18th century it operated as a French-language institution.

berlin-brandenburg-academy-of-sciences-a.name: German Academy of Sciences at Berlin
berlin-brandenburg-academy-of-sciences-a.summary: A predecessor of today's Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences and Humanities, built on earlier academies including East Germany's Academy of Sciences of the German Democratic Republic, founded in 1946.
berlin-brandenburg-academy-of-sciences-a.source_title: Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences and Humanities

ninety-five-theses.name: Ninety-five Theses
ninety-five-theses.summary: A list of propositions written by Martin Luther in 1517 criticizing the sale of indulgences, retrospectively considered to have launched the Protestant Reformation.

pragmatic-sanction-of-1713.name: Pragmatic Sanction of 1713
pragmatic-sanction-of-1713.summary: An edict issued by Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI in 1713 allowing Habsburg lands to pass undivided to a daughter, which let his daughter Maria Theresa later inherit them.

maria-theresa.name: Maria Theresa
maria-theresa.summary: Ruler of the Habsburg monarchy from 1740 to 1780 and the only woman ever to hold that position in her own right, governing territories including Austria, Hungary and Bohemia.

peace-of-westphalia.name: Peace of Westphalia
peace-of-westphalia.summary: Two 1648 treaties that ended the Thirty Years' War, a conflict that killed 4.5 to 8 million people, and are seen as the origin of the modern principle of state sovereignty.

peace-of-augsburg.name: Peace of Augsburg
peace-of-augsburg.summary: An 1555 treaty between Charles V and the Schmalkaldic League letting Holy Roman rulers choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for their states, until the settlement collapsed before the Thirty Years' War.

maximilian-i-holy-roman-emperor.name: Maximilian I
maximilian-i-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor from 1508 (King of the Romans from 1486) who broke tradition by never being crowned by the Pope, expanding Habsburg power through war and marriages that later gave his grandson the thrones of Castile and Aragon.

imperial-government.name: Reichsregiment
imperial-government.summary: Two short-lived attempts, in 1500 and 1521, to create a unified imperial government for the Holy Roman Empire, seated in Nuremberg, which failed due to the emperor's resistance.

reichskammergericht.name: Imperial Chamber Court
reichskammergericht.summary: One of the two highest courts of the Holy Roman Empire, founded in 1495 by the Imperial Diet in Worms and dissolved in 1806.

suleiman-the-magnificent.name: Suleiman the Magnificent
suleiman-the-magnificent.summary: Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566, whose long reign brought the empire's greatest economic, military and political power and reformed its legal system.

siege-of-k-szeg.name: Siege of Güns
siege-of-k-szeg.summary: A 1532 siege in which a tiny Habsburg garrison under Nikola Jurišić held the fort of Kőszeg (Güns) against Suleiman the Magnificent's huge Ottoman army, delaying and turning back his advance on Vienna.

electorate-of-hanover.name: Electorate of Hanover
electorate-of-hanover.summary: A Holy Roman Empire electorate in northwestern Germany, created in 1692, whose ruler became King of Great Britain in 1714 while it remained a separate territory.

house-of-wittelsbach.name: Wittelsbach family
house-of-wittelsbach.summary: A Bavarian dynasty that ruled territories including Bavaria, the Palatinate and, at times, Sweden, Denmark and Hungary, with three members becoming Holy Roman Emperor.

francis-i-holy-roman-emperor.name: Francis I, Holy Roman Emperor
francis-i-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor from 1745 to 1765 and Grand Duke of Tuscany, who became ruler of the Habsburg domains through his marriage to Maria Theresa; the couple had sixteen children.

kasperle.name: Kasperltheater
kasperle.summary: A traditional German-speaking puppet theater dating to the 17th century, so popular that its name became a byword for puppet theater generally, akin to Britain's Mister Punch.

joseph-ii-holy-roman-emperor.name: Joseph II
joseph-ii-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor from 1765 and sole ruler of the Habsburg monarchy from 1780 until his death in 1790, known for enlightened absolutist reforms called Josephinism.

austrian-netherlands.name: Austrian Netherlands
austrian-netherlands.summary: The territory of the Holy Roman Empire's Burgundian Circle from 1714 to 1797, formed when Austria acquired the former Spanish Netherlands, before Revolutionary France annexed it.

electorate-of-bavaria.name: Electorate of Bavaria
electorate-of-bavaria.summary: A hereditary electorate of the Holy Roman Empire from 1623 to 1806, ruled by the Wittelsbach dynasty, later becoming the Kingdom of Bavaria.

charles-theodore-elector-of-bavaria.name: Charles Theodore
charles-theodore-elector-of-bavaria.summary: German nobleman of the House of Wittelsbach (1724–1799) who became Elector Palatine of the Rhine in 1742 and Prince-Elector of Bavaria in 1777.

critique-of-pure-reason.name: Critique of Pure Reason
critique-of-pure-reason.summary: Immanuel Kant's 1781 book examining the limits of metaphysics and reason, responding to Hume's skepticism and Descartes through his theory of transcendental idealism.

critique-of-practical-reason.name: Critique of Practical Reason
critique-of-practical-reason.summary: Immanuel Kant's 1788 'second critique,' a major work of moral philosophy developing his account of a will guided by moral law alone.

critique-of-judgment.name: Critique of Judgment
critique-of-judgment.summary: A 1790 book by philosopher Immanuel Kant, known as his 'third critique,' following his Critique of Pure Reason and Critique of Practical Reason.

transcendental-idealism.name: Transcendental idealism
transcendental-idealism.summary: A philosophical system founded by Immanuel Kant in the 18th century, holding that space and time are forms contributed by the mind rather than existing independently of us.

johann-gottlieb-fichte.name: Fichte
johann-gottlieb-fichte.summary: German philosopher (1762–1814) and founding figure of German idealism, known for his work on self-consciousness; the thesis–antithesis–synthesis idea, often credited to Hegel, actually originated with him.

friedrich-wilhelm-joseph-schelling.name: Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling
friedrich-wilhelm-joseph-schelling.summary: A German philosopher seen as a bridge between Fichte and Hegel in the development of German idealism, whose evolving philosophy is considered difficult to interpret.

georg-wilhelm-friedrich-hegel.name: Hegel
georg-wilhelm-friedrich-hegel.summary: German philosopher (1770–1831) and major figure in German idealism, whose dialectical system, 'absolute idealism,' shaped modern metaphysics, political philosophy and philosophy of religion.

david-hume.name: David Hume
david-hume.summary: A Scottish philosopher, historian and economist (1711–1776) known for his empiricism, arguing that causal reasoning rests on habit and experience rather than pure reason.

baruch-spinoza.name: Baruch Spinoza
baruch-spinoza.summary: 17th-century Dutch philosopher of Portuguese-Jewish origin and forerunner of the Enlightenment, whose ideas shaped modern biblical criticism and rationalist thought.

diet-of-speyer-1529.name: Diet of Speyer (1529)
diet-of-speyer-1529.summary: 1529 assembly of the Holy Roman Empire held in Speyer that reversed an earlier, more tolerant 1526 diet and banned further religious reform, provoking the Protestation at Speyer.

augsburg-confession.name: Augsburg Confession
augsburg-confession.summary: The main statement of Lutheran belief, written in German and Latin and presented to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Augsburg on 25 June 1530.

philipp-melanchthon.name: Philipp Melanchthon
philipp-melanchthon.summary: German Lutheran reformer and collaborator of Martin Luther (1497–1560), the first systematic theologian of the Protestant Reformation and an influential designer of educational systems.

huldrych-zwingli.name: Huldrych Zwingli
huldrych-zwingli.summary: Swiss theologian (1484–1531) who led the Reformation in Switzerland, preaching reform from Zurich's Grossmünster starting in 1519 and introducing a new communion liturgy to replace the Mass in 1525.

cuius-regio-eius-religio.name: Cuius regio, eius religio
cuius-regio-eius-religio.summary: A Latin phrase meaning 'whose realm, his religion,' the principle agreed at the 1555 Peace of Augsburg that a ruler's religion, Catholic or Lutheran, determined that of his subjects.

maximilian-ii-holy-roman-emperor.name: Maximilian II
maximilian-ii-holy-roman-emperor.summary: Holy Roman Emperor from 1564 to 1576 and a Habsburg Catholic who, despite seeking to overcome the Lutheran-Catholic schism, faced ongoing Ottoman wars and tension with his Spanish Habsburg cousins; he lived 1527–1576.

bohemia.name: Bohemia
bohemia.summary: The westernmost and largest historical region of today's Czech Republic, once a duchy and kingdom within the Holy Roman Empire.

wittenberg.name: Wittenberg
wittenberg.summary: German town on the River Elbe closely tied to Martin Luther and the Reformation, where his Ninety-five Theses were published in 1517.

jesuits.name: Jesuits
jesuits.summary: A Catholic religious order founded in Rome in 1540 by Ignatius of Loyola, active worldwide in education, missionary work, charity and humanitarian efforts.

trier-witch-trials.name: Trier witch trials
trier-witch-trials.summary: Witch trials in the diocese of Trier between 1581 and 1593, among the largest documented in history, with about 368 people executed in the city itself.

fulda-witch-trials.name: Fulda witch trials
fulda-witch-trials.summary: A series of witch trials in Fulda, Germany from 1603 to 1606 that killed about 250 people, among the four largest such trials in Germany, ordered by a Counter-Reformation prince-abbot.

eichst-tt-witch-trials.name: Eichstätt witch trials
eichst-tt-witch-trials.summary: A series of witch trials in the Prince-Bishopric of Eichstätt, Bavaria, between 1532 and 1723, resulting in at least 224 executions, among Germany's largest such trials.

bamberg-witch-trials.name: Bamberg witch trials
bamberg-witch-trials.summary: One of the largest witch trials in history, held in the self-governing Catholic Prince-Bishopric of Bamberg in the Holy Roman Empire between 1627 and 1632, in which about 1,000 people were executed.

w-rzburg-witch-trials.name: Würzburg witch trials
w-rzburg-witch-trials.summary: Mass witch trials in the Prince-Bishopric of Würzburg from 1625 to 1631, resulting in hundreds of executions and ranking among the largest witch trials in history.

philipp-adolf-von-ehrenberg.name: Philipp Adolf von Ehrenberg
philipp-adolf-von-ehrenberg.summary: Prince-Bishop of Würzburg from 1622 to 1631 who oversaw the Würzburg witch trials, in which about 900 accused witches were executed.

f-hr.name: Föhr
f-hr.summary: A North Frisian island off Germany's North Sea coast, formed in 1362 when a storm flood split the mainland coastline; it belonged to Denmark until 1864, when it passed to Prussia.
